subject: blueprintSpitfire
pitch:
Category: Vehicle.
Subject: Spitfire fighter plane.
Style: cyanotype blueprint.
reasoning:
I'm thinking a cyanotype blueprint-style Spitfire could be a static prop, but adding a simple root joint with a propeller joint might make it feel more alive without needing a full rig.

For the look, I'll go deep Prussian blue with white panel lines, rivets, roundels, and labels like "SUPERMARINE SPITFIRE Mk.I" drawn as white line art, plus dimension annotations to sell the technical drawing feel. I'm working out real-world proportions (length ~9.12m, wingspan ~11.23m, height ~3.86m) and figuring out the fuselage tilt for a grounded three-point stance, leaning toward keeping it simple with a mild nose-up angle or even level for ease.

Now I'm nailing down the propeller geometry and ground clearance, plus gear placement and wheel track, calculating thrust-line height so the prop tip stays clear of the ground and positioning the splayed main gear legs under the wings based on Spitfire's actual track width.

Next I'm working out the elliptical wing planform—using the span and area to derive the root chord via the ellipse area formula, since the Spitfire's wing was famously elliptical in shape.

Working out the extrude geometry isn't quite right for tapering airfoil thickness along the span, since a single extrude only varies thickness along the chord direction, not span. I'm considering switching to a loft approach instead, with cross-section stations at different span positions to get the proper taper.

I think I can set up the sweep with an `up: [0,1,0]` vector so the tangent-normal-binormal frame orients ry (thickness) along world up and rx (chord) along the Z-ish binormal axis—that should give the elliptical cross-section the right orientation along the wing's span.

But I realize an elliptical cross-section rounds both leading and trailing edges, which isn't quite right for a wing—I need a shift offset so the centerline sits at quarter-chord rather than mid-chord, and I need to reconsider whether ellipse is really the right section shape given Spitfire-style taper from 13% root thickness to 6% tip thickness.

For dihedral, I'm curving the wing path upward from root to tip using a catmull spline, with the tip rounding naturally to zero radius via a sqrt falloff so it tapers into a smooth elliptical point.

Now working out the actual chord geometry: for the elliptical planform I need leading and trailing edge ellipses positioned around the straight quarter-chord line, with the midpoint offset by roughly a quarter chord in world z, though I'm unsure yet which sign the binormal shift should take relative to the sweep path.

I'll build each wing as a separate catmull-rom path per side (s=+1 left, s=-1 right), starting from the fuselage root, approximating the parameter along the path as roughly linear in x since the curve stays nearly straight. I'm computing the chord-based thickness envelope along that path to shape the wing's cross-section.

For armament detail, I'm planning the wing gun layout -- four machine guns per side for the Mk I's eight Brownings, with later variants swapping in a mix of Hispano cannons and .303 stubs along the leading edge, plus aileron lines, flaps, and wingtip lights for added realism.

I also want to add the Type B roundel decal on the upper wing, drawn as concentric circles with blue fill and white outlines to match the blueprint aesthetic.

Now I'm moving to the fuselage, planning a loft with defined stations capturing the round nose cowling, cockpit section, and tapering tail toward the rudder post. I'm setting the overall length near 9.1 units, placing the spinner tip forward near z=3.55 and the tail end near z=-5.6, with the thrust axis sloped slightly along the centerline to match the Spitfire's profile.

I'm working out the fuselage cross-section heights and centerlines at different points along its length—cowl, firewall, cockpit—and trying to capture the characteristic Spitfire top line with its cowl bump, windscreen, and canopy rise against the underside radiator bulge.

Checking wing root clearance against the belly line: at z=0.5 the underside sits near 1.16, which intersects the low-mounted wing thickness reasonably well, though the ground clearance feels a bit high compared to a real tail-down stance. I'm nudging the mid-fuselage stations slightly lower to account for the ~5° nose-to-tail slope.

Now I'm working through the landing gear geometry—checking if the leg length from the wing underside down to the wheel center matches a realistic ~1.0 unit strut, accounting for the wide wheel track and outward-angled placement, plus factoring in how wing dihedral shifts the underside height at the gear attachment point.

I'm uncertain of the exact undercarriage track figure, so I'm cross-checking against photos instead, where the wheels appear to sit roughly a third of the way out along the semi-span rather than half, suggesting a narrower track than my initial estimate—settling on something closer to x ≈ ±1.95 m for now.

With that fixed, I'm modeling the gear leg itself: an angled oleo strut running from the wing root area down and outward to the wheel hub, including the fork, tire, hub disc details, and the small leg fairing door that sits flush against the outer surface. I'm working out the leg's length by comparing the wing's underside height at that spanwise position to the wheel's resting height on the ground.

Then I'm turning to the tailwheel assembly—placing a strut from the belly of the fuselage down to a small tailwheel near the tail, figuring out proportions so the strut length and wheel radius look right, while reconsidering that in reality a tailwheel-equipped aircraft sits nose-high with the tail noticeably lower, so the strut needs to be longer than a naive level-fuselage calculation would suggest.

I decide instead of fully rotating the model to simulate the tail-down attitude, it's simpler to slope the fuselage centerline itself—raising the nose and lowering the tail by roughly 8 degrees—then size the tailplane and tailwheel strut accordingly. I'm weighing whether to tilt the propeller disc to match the thrust-line angle or just keep it vertical for simplicity, leaning toward building the fuselage along this sloped line as a consistent reference for everything else.

I'm working out the rotation formulas for the tilt transform, so nose-up pitch maps z and y coordinates through a pivot point correctly. Since the whole aircraft pitches together, wings need the same tilt applied, which means mapping their sweep paths through this transform while keeping the sweep frame orientation consistent with the "up" vector.

I'll define helper functions that transform points and directions through the pivot-based rotation, so all geometry can be built in simple level coordinates and mapped through this helper for both positions and orientations—keeping the code clean for extrudes and sections. Setting pitch angle to 9 degrees and identifying the pivot point for the rotation.

I need to work out where the wheel contact points land in world coordinates so the ground clearance comes out right—placing the wing, gear, and prop center consistently relative to the tilted thrust axis so the wheels actually touch down at the correct height.

Solving for Yw gives about -1.386, meaning the wheel centre sits roughly 1.39 below the thrust line at the wing station -- but that leaves almost no leg length against the wing underside, way too tight. I'm second-guessing the geometry and considering realistic propeller clearance and thrust line height values to sanity-check this against an actual 3-point stance.

Wing sits right at the fuselage bottom, confirming a low-wing layout. I'm now solving for the wheel offset and reference height using the pitch angle formula, getting H0 ≈ 1.437, then applying that to find the propeller centre position at the nose station.

Checking propeller clearance next: with a 1.6 radius disc tilted about 9°, the lowest point comes out around 0.40 and the top near 3.56-3.86, which looks acceptable. Then I'm working through the wing's vertical position at the dihedral station, landing gear leg length, and how the wheel well geometry needs to accommodate roughly a 0.55 length allowance.

Now I'm solving for the tail wheel position, converting between the tilted design frame and world coordinates to find where the tail wheel centerline sits relative to the fuselage taper near the tail.

Checking the tail fin and fuselage dimensions overall — nose-to-tail length of 9.15 looks right, and I'm confirming the model faces correctly in world X before moving to work out the full design-to-world tilt transformation.

Still writing helper functions...

Beyond that, I'm thinking through the joint hierarchy—body as root, propeller as a "fan" role joint, and control surfaces like ailerons/rudder/elevators as hinge joints, since this is a vehicle rather than a creature so most parts can stay as plain scenery objects while only the moving surfaces need actual bones.

For the tail, I'll give the fin a fixed mount, the rudder a vertical hinge joint, and the elevators their own joints, all built as flat extruded plates. For wing control surfaces, I'll skip separate hinge geometry since it risks z-fighting, and instead fake panel lines for ailerons/flaps directly in the paint function using position data, accounting for sweep and tilt in model space.

Then I'm designing a generic blueprint-style paint: a base blue gradient, faint 0.25m grid lines on dominant faces, rivet dots along seams, and I'm considering reusing a "panelled" helper with a light blue-white seam colour and a yellow-ish bevel highlight for glint effects.

Now I'm working out the grid overlay math: major lines every 0.5m, minor every 0.1m at lower alpha, then calculating texel resolution against total surface area (~80m²) to pick a paint size around 2048 so grid lines stay crisp at roughly 1-2cm per texel.

I'm also thinking about adding white highlight strips along the leading edge to mimic a cyanotype blueprint look, working out which angular sector of the wing sweep corresponds to the leading edge based on direction of travel along the wing.

I'll convert normals and positions to local design space, then sketch out a set of 5-12 decal textures to build — starting with a roundel design as concentric rings rendered as transparent cutouts so the base color shows through in a hatched pattern.

For the roundel I'm thinking of drawing it as outlined rings in pale blue-white and white tones, mimicking the Spitfire's blue-white-red-yellow cockade but flattened into cyanotype monochrome, plus fuselage squadron code letters alongside the roundel.

I'm also planning a dimension-arrow decal on the wing upper surface, with "SPITFIRE Mk I — 11.23 m" lettered in blueprint style alongside span measurement arrows, similar to technical drawing annotations.

For the cockpit, I'm designing the canopy as a translucent light-cyan glazed shape built from a windscreen frustum and a sliding hood loft, with thin darker-blue frame lines painted at specific intervals to simulate the metal canopy ribs.

Moving to the propeller, I'm planning tapered blade extrusions with a white tip-band texture covering the last 15% of each blade, plus a spiral-striped lathed spinner. For the exhausts, I'm considering six small Merlin-style stub pipes per side with a subtle cyan glow effect, possibly extending the glow treatment to the gunsight reflector glass too.

I'll skip any title-block or ground elements and dimension-line decorations since nothing else should surround the model, though decal stripes acting as dimension lines on the fuselage could work well. I'm adding rivet and panel-line texture to the tailplane via paint, honeycomb grid texture for the underwing radiator and oil-cooler intakes, star-spoke hub texture for the wheels with chevron tread on the tires, and skipping the gun-port stencils, then moving on to the pitot tube.

Now I'm placing the pitot tube on the left wing and an aerial mast on the fuselage with a thin antenna wire sweeping from mast to fin tip, plus the "K9942" serial text near the tail. For textures I'll need roundels for wing and fuselage, code letters, serial numbers, dimension arrows, honeycomb, and wheel hub patterns — and I'm deciding to add a simple cockpit interior (seat, headrest armor plate, instrument panel with gauges) visible through the tinted canopy glass rather than a full pilot figure.

I'm rethinking the canopy itself: rather than modeling full interior detail, I'll build it as a frame structure with glass panels, possibly using a stretched/scaled half-ellipsoid dome geometry textured with painted frame lines so the glass reads as transparent where needed.

Since full cutouts aren't achievable with transparency, I'll fake glass by drawing fine diagonal hatching lines across the glass area, like a blueprint pattern, which lets the interior show through the gaps while still looking like glazing. Since textured parts only render front faces, this works fine for viewing the hood from outside -- I'll use a partial sphere with thetaStart and thetaLength set to carve out just the needed quarter dome shape.

Now I'm thinking through how UV coordinates map onto that partial sphere, since the drawing texture needs to stretch correctly over the kept hemisphere -- mapping azimuth to u and polar angle to v so the bottom edge of the drawing lines up with the equator and the top lines up with the pole.

I'm placing the long axis of the hood ellipsoid along Z, so u=0.25 corresponds to the forward (+Z) direction and u=0.75 to the rear, letting me plan vertical ribs as frame lines across the canopy at fixed u positions.

Rethinking the rib geometry: transverse frames should run along lines of constant z rather than following meridians, since meridians converge at the poles on an elongated shape. That suggests using a lathe operation around the z-axis to generate the canopy's circular cross-section, though I need to check whether lathe supports scaling and painted frame details versus just producing an opaque glass surface.

Alternatively, I could orient a sphere so its pole axis aligns with local Z, letting the equator become the opening and the pole become the rounded nose tip -- effectively producing a half-ellipsoid dome with the ribs fanning naturally around that axis.

Actually a full hollow canopy with ribs and tinted glass panels is overengineering; I'll settle for a loft-based hood with painted frame lines and a light cyan opaque glass tone, giving that blueprint-glass look without a fully modeled skeleton.

I'm planning out the full module now — imports from the SDK (frame, line, rng, aim, offset, catmull, bezier, polyline, arc, paint, noise, mix, smoothstep, svg) plus the glow kit, aiming for an efficient ~700-900 line build.

I'm setting up the builder with a restrained flat blueprint palette (deep blues, pale cyans, white) and sketching a reusable paint function that computes a local inverse-transformed coordinate to drive the hull's grid lines, seams, and rivet detailing.

Now I'm computing the base tone as a lightness gradient tied to the surface normal's y-component, layering subtle grain noise for texture and larger blotch noise to mimic uneven cyanotype exposure across the panel.

For drawing lines, I'm projecting coordinates onto the dominant plane based on the surface's major normal axis, then overlaying a minor grid every 0.1 units (thin, faint) and a major grid every 0.5 units (slightly bolder), plus panel seam lines and rivet rows for structural detail. I'm weighing whether the projected grid looks too busy on curved surfaces versus a proper blueprint page, deciding to keep the major grid subtle while treating panel lines and rivets as the primary drawing marks -- on wings specifically, panel lines run chordwise using x/z coordinate multiples since the dominant normal there is y.

Now I'm moving to fuselage construction: a loft through stations defined by position, width, and height, with each station's orientation tilted according to a path tangent, and I'm considering what cross-section shape (circle, ellipse, or box) and orientation frame to use as the loft sweeps along the body's path.

I'm deciding between 12-sided flat facets with smooth shading off for that low-poly fuselage look, since paint baking will still handle tone via normals. For the rig, I'll set up a joint hierarchy with a root body, a propeller joint at the nose, and hinge joints for the rudder and elevator surfaces.

For ailerons, overlaying a thin raised plate on the wing's trailing edge would create an obvious patch-like seam, so I'm opting to skip separate aileron joints entirely and instead suggest their presence through paint seams based on local coordinate ranges on the wing.

I'm also marking the flap region further inboard and noting that wing paint positions only need x and z since dihedral doesn't significantly shift those values. For the rudder and elevator, I'm including their hinge joints so plates attach correctly, with the rudder hinged about a vertical axis near the tail.

Now I'm setting up the propeller joint along its spin axis with the spinner lathed around that same direction and blades extruded radially. I also need a root body joint with no parent, then plan a helper function to simplify part placement by defaulting to the body bone unless a part needs to move with a specific joint.

For sweeps and lofts, explicit bone assignment takes priority, so I'm confirming those will attach correctly to the body or relevant joint. Now I'm working out wing geometry, computing coordinates mirrored across both sides with a path that curves based on a sweep angle, laying out the spanwise points and their vertical offset using a shallow tangent slope.

I'm also placing the quarter-chord line along z to position the wing root and tip, working out leading and trailing edge offsets so the wing sits correctly relative to the nose, tail, and cockpit, with the canopy positioned roughly over the wing's trailing edge region.

Working out fuselage cross-section stations from tail to nose, tracking center height, width, and depth at each point along the body so the wing and fuselage blend smoothly underneath.

I'll use flat/point caps for the loft similar to sweep options, assuming shared API. Now I'm working out the fuselage cross-section heights along the spine, tracking how the top and bottom edges shift from nose to tail relative to the thrust line to match the Spitfire's silhouette.

I'm thinking through the tail section geometry more carefully — the belly line should rise slightly toward the tail, and I'm adjusting the vertical center position there to roughly match real Spitfire proportions near the tailwheel strut.

Checking the tail wheel's actual world-space height using the fuselage transform, I find the bottom edge sits almost exactly at ground level, so I'm nudging the vertical offset slightly to get a small clearance instead of touching zero.

Working through the wheel geometry: solving for design-space y using the world z offset and tilt angle gives yl around -1.166 for the wheel center. Then I'm figuring out the main gear leg attachment point on the wing underside, using the wing's spanwise y-position function to locate where the strut connects near x=1.45.

I'm now laying out the oleo leg structure itself — an outer cylinder for the upper strut, a thinner chrome inner piston for the lower section, plus fork plates flanking the wheel and axle, and planning a teardrop-shaped outer door fairing extruded along the leg's outward direction to match the Spitfire's characteristic gear door shape.

Instead I'll separate the hub texture from the tire geometry—using circle textures on the outward-facing sides plus a cylinder band for the hub, and building the tire itself as a lathe-rotated profile around the axle axis to get a rounded torus-like shape.

Writing tread and hub texture code...

Now I'm adding the tail wheel assembly with its small tire, fork rod, and oleo strut dropping from the belly. For the engine, I'm sketching cowl bulges and exhaust stacks—six small glowing stub rods per side spaced along the cowl, angled aft-outward for a realistic exhaust look.

I'm also detailing the cowl ring as a closed swept torus for the front lip, then building the spinner as a lathe profile tapering from a rounded base to a pointed tip, positioned just ahead of the cowl to sit behind the prop.

Now I'm designing the three-blade propeller, shaping each blade's outline with a narrow root, a broad mid-section widening toward the tip, and a rounded tip profile, using radial coordinates around the hub axis.

I'm working out how to orient each blade with proper pitch by rotating the chord direction about the radial axis, then computing the thickness direction from the cross product, and placing the hub along the fuselage axis. I'm also adding tip paint bands based on a surface coordinate check.

Now I'm designing the cockpit canopy and windscreen — building a flat, steeply raked front windscreen panel plus curved side glazing as a lofted shape, defining cross-section stations (position, width, height) moving from the windscreen base back along the fuselage.

I see the gap, so I'm lowering the canopy's center to y=0.6 with height 0.52 so it properly overlaps the fuselage, peaking around 0.88 for a realistic windscreen height above the cowl. Now I'm adjusting the other canopy stations to line up with the cowl top near 0.5-0.55.

The canopy tail merges into the fuselage turtledeck further aft. For the glass, I'm planning pale-cyan canopy panes with white frame lines marking the windscreen bow and sliding hood bars, keeping contrast low for a blueprint look.

Skipping the pilot figure since the seat is hidden, I'll add small glowing details instead: wingtip nav lights, exhaust glow, and a tiny reflector gunsight box with a glowing ring mounted just ahead of the windscreen. I'm also placing a short radio aerial mast behind the canopy near the top of the fuselage.

Now I'm working out the radiator placement under the wings—oil cooler on one side, glycol radiator on the other, as tapered scoop boxes positioned near the wheel wells roughly symmetrical about the fuselage.

I'll add a honeycomb-textured plane at the front intake face of the frustum box, keeping the ends flat and square to the axis since the box maps through the tilt transform. Then I'm placing gun stubs along each wing at roughly x=2.4, 2.75, 3.1, 3.45, positioning them relative to the leading-edge curve.

For wingtips, I'm adding rounded sweeps with a small glowing sphere nav light at each tip—cyan on the left, pale white on the right—plus a pitot tube rod protruding forward from the left wing's underside near x=3.8.

Now for the tail fin, I'm setting up a side-view extrusion where the outline runs along the fuselage's top-down z-axis (forward-back) and vertically along y, with thickness extending laterally along x. I'm defining the fin's base along the fuselage spine starting around z=-3.

Sketching the rounded rudder shape with a straight leading edge sweeping back into a curved top, trying several point sets to capture the characteristic Spitfire Mk I tail silhouette before settling on coordinates for the fixed fin and separate hinge line for the rudder.

Continuing the rudder outline down to the bottom, tucked near the fuselage tail end, and considering the bulbous lower curve typical of the Spitfire Mk I rudder. I'm adding bevel thickness and painting horizontal rib lines across the fabric surface using the s-coordinate to mimic the fabric-covered control surface look.

Now moving to the tailplane: designing an elliptical shape similar to the wing, span 3.2 with a 1.1 root chord, mounted at the fuselage side. I'm setting up the outline in the plan view with the span direction along x and chord along z, computing the proper orthogonal thickness direction, and positioning the mount point before mirroring for the left side.

Working out the elliptical chord profile and leading-edge sweep for the tailplane geometry...

For the tip, the TE duplicate point gets dropped since it matches the LE tip exactly. For the elevator, I'll split the tailplane outline into a fixed section ahead of the hinge line and a movable elevator section behind it, dividing at roughly the midchord.

I'm thinking through the elliptical tail geometry accounting for the fuselage width at the root, then considering whether to use the same sweep/extrude technique for the wings as for the tail, favoring a sweep approach for proper thickness and rounded tips, with ailerons and flaps marked as painted lines rather than separate geometry.

Now I'm deciding against adding a cockpit headrest detail, and planning the fuselage decals—placing roundels symmetrically on both sides via a sweep-based decal with mirrored direction vectors, then positioning the squadron code letters ("QV") and individual aircraft letter relative to the roundel position along the fuselage, following typical Spitfire marking conventions.

Placing wing decals...

I need the dimension decal with the "5.61" label to curve properly across the dihedral wing tilt, so I'm working out the projection geometry—figuring out which screen direction corresponds to "right" when viewed from above with the camera looking down and forward pointing up on screen.

Working through the orientation, screen-right ends up being -x, which means text on each wing should read toward the fuselage (toward -x), consistent for both wings when viewed from behind-above looking forward—mirroring as needed. With parts count tracking toward 180-340, I'm now considering adding a cowling fastener ring detail near the nose.

Adding cowl rivet rings...

Actually I'm reconsidering the part budget — studding 28 rivets per loop across multiple stations gets expensive fast, so I'll skip individual rivet parts and rely on painted bands plus maybe a sparse row on the spinner backplate instead.

Tallying up rough part counts: fuselage, cowl ring, spinner, backplate, three blades, canopy, sight, wings, tailplanes, fin, rudder, landing gear per side (legs, fork, axle, tire, hub, door), tail wheel, exhausts, guns, radiators, bands, mast/wire/pitot, decals, nav lights — this lands somewhere around 120 parts, so I have a bit of room to add cowl bulges or fastener details without blowing the limit.

Thinking about remaining fiddly extras: elevator trim tabs, wing root fillets, oil cooler grill, the chin intake scoop under the nose, exhaust shrouds, engine bearers. I'll skip the gun bulges and cartouche text ideas since they're not essential, though a thin centerline construction rod through the fuselage could be a nice blueprint-style touch.

I'm tallying up the textures needed: roundel, fuselage roundel variant, code letters QV, the K letter, walkway "NO STEP" text, dimension arrow, honeycomb pattern, hub, and serial number — about nine total, keeping the flat color count under 64.

Setting up trigonometric constants for the paint calculations...

Defining the forward and inverse transform helpers that rotate points and normals by the tilt angle, then verifying the inverse of the rotation transform algebraically checks out.

Now I'm building a reusable hull-painting helper that takes options like panel bounds, rivets, grid lines, and a seed, returning a paint function that blends colors based on position and normal using the SDK's mix utility.

Adding fine grain and axis selection logic...

Computing rivet placement along seams using fractional distance functions, then estimating surface area across wings, fuselage, and tail to figure out texel density—around 186 texels per meter, roughly 5.4mm each, which means the seam width should be about 0.01 to stay crisp.

I'm now working out the hull geometry for painted panels like ailerons and flap hinges, defining line conditions based on chord position and relative span to mark hinge boundaries on the wing.

Then I'm shifting to roundel textures, setting up the SVG viewbox and sketching out the concentric circles with their colors for the wing roundel design.

Adding crosshair overlay lines and a subtle dashed circle, then layering the fuselage roundel rings with a pale-to-deep blue cyanotype palette, keeping everything within the blue-and-white scheme.

Now I'm generating the small decal elements: the "QV" lettering mark, the rear serial code, a stenciled "NO STEP" walkway label, and a dimension arrow line with arrowheads on both ends.

Writing honeycomb pattern...

Then I'll design the hub as a circular SVG with concentric rings, bolt holes, and spoke lines radiating from a center cap, all in deep blue and white tones to match the wheel's metallic look. For the canopy glass, I'm blending a gradient base color with paint frame strips positioned at specific angles across the surface.

Designing a spiral stripe pattern for the spinner using banded angle-height modulation, then moving to the prop blades with white tip bands and dark blue bases for contrast.

Now I'm working out the wing geometry: half-span 5.6 units with a tapered chord of 2.55 at root, a slight 6° dihedral slope, and thickness tapering from 13% to lower values outward. I'm plotting sweep points along the span and checking the chord shrinks elliptically near the tip, ending around 5.5 with a rounded cap where the remaining chord is small.

I'm placing denser sample points near the wingtip where chord shrinks fastest, computing the mid-chord z positions, and smoothing with a catmull curve. The ellipse radii (rx, ry) scale with chord width and a tapering thickness ratio, and I'm checking that both wing paths meet correctly at the centerline inside the fuselage.

For the sweep direction I'm setting up as the y-axis vector, confirming the path accepts Vector3 points from the catmull spline, and bumping the cross-section sides from the default octagon to ten for a smoother lens shape. For the fuselage loft I'm defining stations with position, width, and height, attaching it to the body bone, applying the paneled hull paint, and capping the ends.

Now I'm adding nose details: an elliptical cowling cross-section (narrower at front), a chin-mounted intake scoop below the nose for the carb air intake using a tapered box shape with a honeycomb texture, while skipping any cannon blister bulges on the cowl top.

I'm also adding exhaust stacks—six per side as small rod-shaped stubs embedded near the fuselage surface around z=1.45 to 2.5, evenly spaced to mimic the Spitfire's characteristic fishtail exhaust groupings.

For guns, I'm using thin pale rods along the wing. For nav lights, small glowing spheres sit at the wingtips, and I'm planning a mast sweep for the aerial from the fuselage top.

Now I'm placing the aerial mast slightly raked back near the top of the fuselage, with the wire sagging from mast tip to fin top using a tiny-radius swept rod with few sides. I'm adding a pitot tube as a thin rod under the left wing leading edge, and skipping the pilot/seat detail for now while considering the canopy.

I'm deciding against extra details like head armor or a cockpit door outline, keeping things mostly to paint lines and decals, then working out the landing gear attachment point and wheel center coordinates with tilt adjustments.

Now I'm detailing the oleo leg geometry: outer rod from the attach point to a midpoint, a chrome piston continuing to the wheel, and a fork straddling the wheel with arms offset along x to match the wheel's width.

I'm also adding the gear door covering the wheel's outboard side as an elongated plate positioned slightly outward from the wheel centre, running from the wing down toward the axle.

I'm extending the door outline down near the wheel axle region, smoothing the tapered shape, and working out the door's orientation vectors so it leans outward along the leg's tilt direction.

Checking that the door position stays outboard of the wheel on both ends of its slope — looks correct relative to the wheel's outer face. Now I'm working out the wheel hub decals, placing circle geometry at the wheel centers offset slightly outward on each side, oriented along the x-axis to face outward properly.

Moving to the tail wheel: positioning its lathe-built tire at the tail location with similar radius/width parameters, then connecting the fork rod from the strut bottom down to the wheel center. I'm placing the tail strut's base against the fuselage belly, adjusting its z-position so it lines up with the belly curve at that fuselage station, and working out the top attachment point of the strut.

I'm skipping fillets between wing and fuselage for now since the fuselage already intersects the wing geometry reasonably. For the tailplane, I'm using an elliptical outline helper to build the shape, sizing it to match the real Spitfire's roughly 3-meter span and positioning its quarter-chord line so the leading and trailing edges line up correctly near the rudder.

I'm working out hinge positions for the elevator and rudder so they don't overlap awkwardly—keeping the elevator trailing edge forward of the rudder hinge line, with the rudder extending further aft. I'm placing the tailplane at a y-offset to sit properly relative to the fuselage centerline, then starting to define the elevator joint connecting it to the body.

Setting hinge joint positions...

For elevators ribs run chordwise at x intervals instead, and I'll keep the paint callback signature consistent across parts. I'm also setting up decals on the fuselage loft using target/texture/placement options, and defining fuselage seam loops with a point and direction for the surface.

Now I'm adding sweep-based trim rings — a white cowl lip at the nose, a firewall ring, and tail bands — plus working out the nose cap and prop backplate geometry behind the spinner.

Verifying spinner-to-blade proportions and overall fuselage length (tail to spinner tip ≈ 9.17 units), then moving on to defining the color palette for different aircraft parts.

Renaming cosine/sine helper variables to avoid conflicts, then assigning slightly varied blue-tone palettes to wings, fuselage, and tail for visual depth, plus flat colors for smaller parts like the landing gear. Now checking how decal targets map onto surface sweeps.

Setting up the imports from the builder library, keeping only what's actually used since the typechecker flags unused imports.

Now I'm defining coordinate transform helpers: a fixed dihedral tilt angle, and functions that convert local wing-panel coordinates into world space by rotating around the tilt axis, plus an inverse that recovers design-space Y from world Y given a local Z offset.

With these in place, I'm sketching a paint/hull builder that adds rivet-like seam patterns along panel surfaces, wrapping a periodic pitch value to space them evenly and defining an optional extra callback for per-point color overrides based on position and normal.

Adding wing geometry helpers...

Adding hinge and seam lines for ailerons and flaps...
